strategies.summary: Exploit inference-only BatchNorm semantics by folding `bn1`, `bn2`, and the shortcut BN into adjacent convolutions so the block reduces standalone normalization launches and exposes simpler conv epilogues to cuDNN; this is attractive because the current profile is dominated by cuDNN conv kernels while the prior add+ReLU fusion already removed cheap pointwise work.
implementation_hints: Keep `ModelNew` I/O unchanged and gate the fast path to eval/inference semantics that use running mean/variance rather than per-batch statistics.
Materialize folded conv weights/biases for `conv1`, `conv2`, and the downsample conv using the exact BatchNorm epsilon and affine parameters.
Bypass `forward_stmt_4` and `forward_stmt_7` on the folded path, and replace the downsample `conv+bn` pair with a single folded conv call in `forward_stmt_8`.
Prefer reusing cached folded tensors unless module parameters or running stats change to avoid per-forward recomputation overhead.
strategies.expected_gain: High single-digit to low double-digit percent if BN kernels are currently distinct and folding also improves conv epilogue selection; larger than additional pointwise-only tweaks.
risk_notes: Only safe when preserving inference semantics exactly; do not apply during training or when BatchNorm must compute batch statistics.
Must preserve normalized axes, epsilon, affine state, output dtype, and tensor shapes exactly.
Need a robust cache invalidation story if weights or running stats can mutate after construction.
memory_methods: Eliminate reads/writes for separate BN outputs.
Store folded weights/biases once and reuse across launches.
mutation_axes: eval-only fast path vs fallback path
cached folded parameters vs on-demand folding
fold `bn2` alone vs fold all three normalization sites
forbidden_patterns: Do not recompute BatchNorm statistics over different axes.
Do not change convolution stride/padding/groups or shortcut topology.
Do not fold BN in training mode or ignore affine/bias terms.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Strongest option if this path is inference/eval-only. Folding BatchNorm into adjacent convolutions preserves the required axes/epsilon semantics under running-stat inference, removes standalone normalization work entirely, and aligns with the profile note that conv-heavy execution dominates. Main risk is mode gating and cache invalidation, but risk-adjusted value is still excellent.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Highest-value strategy. BN folding into convs at inference time is well-established, eliminates multiple kernel launches, and can improve cuDNN epilogue selection. Risk is manageable with a clean eval-only gate and parameter cache. The expected gain estimate is realistic given conv dominance in the profile.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Folding BatchNorm into Convolution weights and biases is a highly effective, zero-overhead optimization for inference. It completely eliminates the BN memory traffic and kernel launch overhead.

strategies.summary: Extend the successful epilogue fusion by folding the final normalization affine into the existing residual `add_relu` CUDA path, turning `bn2 -> add -> relu` into one CUDA epilogue over the conv2 output and shortcut tensor.
implementation_hints: Keep `conv2` as cuDNN, then launch one custom kernel that reads the conv output, applies the exact BatchNorm transform using running stats and affine parameters, adds `identity`, and applies ReLU in place or into the existing output buffer.
Preserve the current contiguity/layout guards that made `n5` correct; add a clean fallback to `bn2` plus existing fused add+ReLU when preconditions fail.
Specialize for NCHW contiguous float32 first, with vectorized loads only when alignment and channel packing are valid.
Pass epsilon, running mean/var, and affine parameters explicitly so the fused kernel matches module semantics exactly.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate; likely a few more percent by removing one more full-tensor read/write pair beyond the already-profitable residual epilogue fusion.
risk_notes: This must use the exact normalized channel axis and BatchNorm inference formula; any mismatch breaks correctness.
Training-mode BatchNorm should not be silently routed through an inference-style fused kernel.
Current profile shows convs dominate, so upside is bounded unless BN launches are still prominent.
memory_methods: Fuse BN affine, residual add, and ReLU into one streaming pass.
Reuse the conv2 output buffer to avoid an extra allocation.
mutation_axes: in-place epilogue vs separate output buffer
shortcut contiguous-only fast path vs general fallback
forbidden_patterns: Do not fuse by approximating variance or changing epsilon.
Do not require unconditional `.contiguous()` materialization on every call.
Do not alter the existing successful residual-add semantics from `n5`.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Good targeted fusion. It preserves cuDNN conv performance while removing a full BN-affine pass plus residual add/ReLU traffic at the tail. Lower upside than full folding because convs still dominate, and correctness depends on exact inference BN semantics plus a safe fallback, but this is still a practical, relatively bounded optimization.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Solid incremental win that extends already-proven epilogue fusion. Fusing bn2+add+relu into one streaming pass removes a full-tensor read/write pair. Risk is low given the existing working epilogue infrastructure. Upside is bounded since convs dominate, but the implementation path is clear and correctness constraints are well-understood.

implementation_hints: Convert module weights and activations to channels-last on the fast path and keep them in that format through `conv1`, `conv2`, and the downsample branch to avoid repeated layout transforms.
Only use the path when input and shortcut can remain channels-last end-to-end; otherwise fall back rather than paying conversion cost each layer.
Audit the custom `add_relu` extension so it either accepts channels-last contiguous tensors correctly or is bypassed when its current contiguous assumptions imply NCHW-only behavior.
Use the forward call site to preserve layout consistency across the residual branch and main branch before the epilogue.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate but shape-dependent; potentially meaningful because the Nsight profile shows cuDNN conv kernels dominate and occupancy is register-limited rather than memory-stalled.
risk_notes: Benefit depends on cuDNN kernel selection for this exact `(N,C,H,W)` shape; gratuitous format conversions can erase gains.
Need to respect PyTorch contiguity semantics since channels-last contiguity differs from default contiguous.
Custom CUDA kernels written for flat contiguous memory may need explicit layout validation.
memory_methods: Avoid NCHW<->NHWC ping-pong by committing to one fast-path layout across the full block.
Leverage channels-last contiguous tensors for coalesced conv access patterns.

forbidden_patterns: Do not insert repeated `contiguous()`/format conversions around every op.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Plausibly useful because the workload is conv-dominated and channels-last can improve cuDNN kernel selection, but gains are highly shape/layout dependent and can be erased by format conversions or incompatibility with the custom epilogue. Worth exploring, but not as directly aligned to the normalization-focused anchors as BN folding/fusion.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Channels-last layout can unlock better cuDNN kernels and is a legitimate optimization direction. However, the gain is shape-dependent and unpredictable without profiling the exact (N,C,H,W) configuration. The custom add_relu kernel likely has NCHW assumptions that need auditing, adding implementation risk. Worth trying after higher-confidence strategies are validated.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Using channels-last (NHWC) memory format can unlock faster Tensor Core convolution kernels in cuDNN. However, the overhead of layout conversions must be carefully managed to avoid negating the gains.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Could improve the existing add+ReLU kernel a bit, but the profile already says convolutions dominate, so optimizing this secondary kernel likely yields only small end-to-end gains. review_notes.claude-compatible: Improving the add_relu kernel via float4 and pipeline hints is reasonable in isolation, but the profile explicitly shows cuDNN convolutions dominate runtime. Reducing long-scoreboard stalls in add_relu from 5% to 2-3% of a kernel that is not the bottleneck yields negligible end-to-end speedup. Lower priority unless conv optimizations plateau and profiling confirms add_relu becomes visible.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Vectorizing memory accesses (e.g., float4) in the custom add_relu kernel is a standard and effective way to improve memory bandwidth utilization, though the overall speedup will be limited by the convolution runtime.

Replacing cuDNN-backed conv with a custom fused conv+BN(+ReLU) path often loses on modern CUDA unless the shapes are very special, and the normalization semantics must remain exact. Potential upside exists, but risk-adjusted value is weak relative to safer fusion/folding approaches.

The BN fusion idea has merit but is better pursued via epilogue patching (strategy_02/06) than replacing the conv kernel entirely. Risk-adjusted value is low.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Writing a custom CUDA kernel for the entire Conv+BN+ReLU sequence is highly risky and unlikely to outperform highly tuned cuDNN convolution kernels. The implementation complexity is massive for a likely performance regression.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l3_p8_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():
    global _STARK_EXTENSION
    if _STARK_EXTENSION is None:
        _STARK_EXTENSION = load_inline(
            name=_stark_extension_name(),
            cpp_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC),
            cuda_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC),
            functions=None,
            extra_cflags=['-O3'],
            extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3', '--use_fast_math'],
            with_cuda=True,
            verbose=False,
        )
    return _STARK_EXTENSION

# <<<IMPROVE:user_helpers>>>
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

CUDA_CPP_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cpp>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>

// Add pybind exports for custom CUDA entrypoints here.
PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) {}
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

CUDA_CU_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cu>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>
#include <cuda.h>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Add CUDA kernels and exported wrapper functions here.
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

class ModelNew(nn.Module):
    expansion = 1
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1):
        super().__init__()
        # <<<IMPROVE:init_body>>>
        """
                :param in_channels: Number of input channels
                :param out_channels: Number of output channels
                :param stride: Stride for the first convolutional layer
                :param downsample: Downsample layer for the shortcut connection
                """
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=stride, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)
        self.downsample = nn.Sequential(
                    nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels * self.expansion, kernel_size=1, stride=stride, bias=False),
                    nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels * self.expansion),
                )
        self.stride = stride
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

    def forward(self, x):
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_1>>>
        # Baseline fallback keeps the official PyTorch forward path.
        # After implementing CUDA_CPP_SRC / CUDA_CU_SRC, call _stark_get_extension().your_entrypoint(...).
        """
                :param x: Input tensor, shape (batch_size, in_channels, height, width)
                :return: Output tensor, shape (batch_size, out_channels, height, width)
                """
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_2>>>
        identity = x
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_3>>>
        out = self.conv1(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_4>>>
        out = self.bn1(out)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_5>>>
        out = self.relu(out)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_6>>>
        out = self.conv2(out)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_7>>>
        out = self.bn2(out)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_8>>>
        if self.downsample is not None:
                    identity = self.downsample(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_9>>>
        out += identity
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
